generatedProse.concept-context: The School of Sport gives you a ready language for the differences behind team conflict, because sport and exercise psychology sits inside the school. Work on team roles and personality, which you may meet in a psychology or coaching module, names the tendencies that pull people apart: some push a bold idea, others urge caution, and both can be right in part. Used with care, and without boxing people in, this helps you see why a teammate drives a daring plan while another protects the budget, so you respond to the person rather than only the position. Reflecting on that with a judgement, rather than a description, is itself a skill employers in sport value.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport management and development students are in a team where the designer and the analyst are arguing hard over how to pitch a community participation campaign, two days before the presentation.

Tom finds the row stressful and stays quiet, hoping it will pass. Asked later to reflect, he writes that 'there was a disagreement but we sorted it in the end'. The conflict was neither helped nor understood, and the reflection only describes what happened. Nothing was learned that could be carried into the next team.

Amara sees that the designer is an innovator and the analyst a cautious realist, both right in part. She acknowledges each view, then proposes keeping the firm participation figures the analyst wants while adding one bold campaign image the designer suggested. Reflecting afterwards, she writes that stepping in early, and naming the strengths on both sides, was what held the team together, and would do so again. That is a judgement, and it names a transferable skill.

Both saw the same argument. Only Amara resolved it and learned something sayable from it.
generatedProse.summary: Handling conflict in the School of Sport starts with recognising difference, and your school gives you a language for it. Reflecting well means judging your performance, not just describing events, and naming what you have gained. You can now do both, and articulate the transferable-skills value of presenting and group work. With authority, collaboration and reflection in place, you are ready to present and work in teams like a sport graduate.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's reflection a judgement rather than a description?

items.text: It said what she did, why it worked, and what she would do again.
It gave a fuller account of what happened in the meeting.
It was longer than Tom's reflection.
It named the other team members and their roles.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara weighed her own actions and drew a lesson, which is more than description.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what the reflection concluded about Amara's own performance, not how much it described.
feedback.incorrectFinal: It was a judgement because it weighed what Amara did, why it worked, and what she would repeat. A fuller or longer account of events is still description.
